title: Visiting Goindval
hook: the step-well of Guru Amar Das

segments.voice: Yesterday, Muktsar Sahib, where tradition says the Guru tore up the paper of the ones who came back. Your line was the pool of liberation.

The light changes halfway down. At the top of the stairs it's a bright Punjab afternoon, dust and noise and a river nearby. A few steps lower, the walls close in, the air turns cool, and the street drops away. Lower still, there's water, dark and still, at the bottom of a deep shaft of stone. People go down barefoot, one step at a time, some of them saying something under their breath on every step. This is the baoli, the step-well, at Goindval Sahib.
screen: `BRIGHT AT THE TOP.` → `COOL HALFWAY DOWN.` → `WATER AT THE BOTTOM.`

segments.voice: Begin with the place. Goindval is a town on the Beas river, the home of Guru Amar Das, the third Guru. Tradition says he had the baoli dug there, so people could reach water in a dry land, and it became a gathering place for Sikhs. Then the purpose. A step-well is a practical thing: water sits deep below the ground, so you build stairs down to it. But a Guru's well was never only plumbing. Tradition says the water was open to everyone, whatever their caste, and that openness was itself a teaching. Next, the custom. Some pilgrims recite the Japji Sahib once on every step as they go down, slowly, all the way to the water. It is slow on purpose. Finally, the Guru's word underneath. In the Japji, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that along this path are the steps of a stairway, and by climbing them one becomes one with the Lord. The Japji's stairs go up; the well's stairs go down. Both say the same thing about how it's done: not in a leap, but one step, then the next, then the next. The baoli at Goindval Sahib still has its stairs, its water, and its slow walkers.
screen: `A STEP-WELL ON THE BEAS.` · `WATER FOR EVERYONE.` · `THE JAPJI, STEP BY STEP.` · `STAIRS UP, STAIRS DOWN.` · then, large: `STEP BY STEP.`

segments.voice: Go to some stairs if they're near, or take a few slow steps across the room, letting each foot land fully before the next and breathing out on every step. If you know a line of the Japji, say it under your breath as you go; if not, just count your breaths, slower than feels normal.
Visiting Goindval. The town of Guru Amar Das on the Beas, and its baoli, where some pilgrims recite the Japji on every step down to the water. Today's word.
Your line: step by step. Nobody reaches the water in a leap. Go gently.

chat.says: Why do some pilgrims recite the Japji on every step down the Goindval well?
options: It's slow on purpose: like the Japji's stairway, the path is walked one step at a time.
To keep count of the steps, since the well is too dark to see the stairs.
Because the water would be unsafe to touch without a prayer said first.
chat.meaning: Some pilgrims recite the Japji on every step, slowly; the Japji itself speaks of a stairway climbed one step at a time.

notes: Japji pauri 32 (Ang 7): 'eit raahi pat pavaReeaa chaReeai hoi ikees' paraphrased as 'along this path are the steps of a stairway, and by climbing them one becomes one with the Lord'. Please confirm.
The number of steps (tradition says eighty-four) is deliberately not stated (claims rule); the custom is described as 'some pilgrims recite the Japji once on every step'. Please confirm.
'At a time when, in many places, people of different castes were kept away from the same water' is a general historical claim framing the baoli as a teaching; please confirm it is fair.
The langar tradition at Goindval (and Akbar's visit) is deliberately left out to keep one idea.
